title: Research Explained #21 -- When a Simulation Works, What Have We Actually Proven?
html:
Imagine designing a spacecraft on a computer. You enter the equations describing a hypothetical spacetime geometry, run a simulation, and discover that the mathematical model allows a spacecraft to reach a distant destination much faster than light could travel through ordinary space.

The calculations finish successfully. The numerical results appear consistent. Perhaps a second implementation produces the same answers.

Have we discovered faster-than-light travel?

No. But we may have learned something important.

Understanding what that something is—and what it is not—is central to the research we conduct at Beyond the Light Barrier.

A Simulation Is an Experiment on a Model

A physical experiment asks nature a question.

A simulation asks a mathematical model a question.

Both can be valuable, but they provide different kinds of evidence.

Suppose we describe a hypothetical spacetime using equations from general relativity. Those equations specify how distances, time intervals, and the paths of light or matter behave within the assumed geometry.

A simulation can help us investigate questions such as:

  • How would light propagate through this geometry?
  • Would a signal reach a distant observer?
  • How sensitive are the predictions to changes in the model?
  • Would the geometry require unusual distributions of energy and momentum?
  • Does the numerical solution remain stable as we increase its precision?

These are legitimate scientific questions.

But a computer cannot establish that the assumed geometry can actually be constructed.

Even a perfectly implemented simulation cannot make an impossible physical assumption become possible.

Three Different Kinds of Success

It helps to distinguish three milestones that are sometimes confused.

First: The program runs correctly.

The software executes, produces outputs, and passes its tests. This is an important engineering achievement, but it does not establish that the mathematical model is physically correct.

Second: The numerical calculation reproduces the mathematical prediction.

We might compare two numerical methods, increase computational resolution, or verify the output against an analytic result.

Agreement increases our confidence that the numerical methods correctly approximate the stated mathematical problem within the tested conditions and tolerances. It does not eliminate the possibility of shared errors in the equations, assumptions, or implementations.

It does not establish that nature realizes the model.

Third: The prediction survives comparison with physical measurements.

This is where the relationship between a mathematical model and the physical universe is tested.

A properly designed experiment measures a predicted observable, evaluates uncertainty, and investigates conventional explanations.

Even then, one successful measurement may not establish an entire proposed mechanism. The conclusion must remain proportional to the evidence.

An Example From Our Wormhole Communication Research

In our Wormhole Communication (WC) research, we have investigated how hypothetical signals would propagate through specified spacetime geometries.

One line of work, WC-MGT-1, examines carrier propagation under an assumed geometry. The calculations allow us to compare the mathematical behavior of different carrier fields.

This is useful because a proposed communication channel must eventually answer basic questions: Can a signal propagate? Under what assumptions? What determines its transmission characteristics?

Our computational work has produced internally checked results within these models.

But those results do not demonstrate that a traversable wormhole exists, that we can construct one, or that information can actually be transmitted faster than light.

Those are separate physical questions requiring additional evidence.

The distinction matters because a calculation may be correct even when its physical realization remains unknown—or is ultimately ruled out.

An Example From Our Propulsion Research

Our Warp Drive (WD) research encounters a related challenge.

General relativity allows researchers to study many hypothetical spacetime geometries. Some geometries have mathematical properties that motivate investigation of unusual travel possibilities.

However, specifying a geometry is not the same as identifying a physically realizable mechanism for producing it.

A candidate must face questions about its required stress-energy distribution, energy conditions, stability, causal structure, formation and shutdown, and the behavior of matter and radiation.

A successful geometry calculation can reveal requirements or contradictions. It cannot bypass them.

Indeed, discovering that a promising candidate requires conditions that appear incompatible with known physical constraints—or cannot be achieved using any presently established mechanism—could be one of the most valuable results of the investigation.

Why Independent Reproduction Matters

There is another subtle distinction.

Suppose we run the same simulation on an Apple Silicon Mac, an x86-64 Windows computer, and an emulated IBM s390x environment.

If the results agree, we gain evidence that the implementation behaves consistently across the tested computing environments.

That is valuable software verification.

But it is not automatically independent scientific reproduction.

All three executions might share the same incorrect equation, assumption, algorithm, or interpretation.

Independent scientific reproduction requires a sufficiently independent examination of the underlying scientific calculation—not merely running the same program on another computer.

At Beyond the Light Barrier, our documented verification roadmap distinguishes these activities. The roadmap's recorded status does not claim independent scientific reproduction or physical experimental confirmation of our proposed advanced spacetime mechanisms.

What About Negative Results?

Imagine a simulation predicts an extremely small physical effect.

After calculating the expected signal, we discover that it is many orders of magnitude below the sensitivity of available instruments.

Have we failed?

We have not demonstrated the effect experimentally. We may also have shown that the proposed experiment, under its stated assumptions, is not a credible way to detect it.

That is useful knowledge.

It can prevent wasted effort, identify which parameters matter most, and direct future research toward more realistic experiments—or toward a different hypothesis.

A negative result can constrain the search space just as a positive result can motivate further investigation.

Our goal is not to make every proposed mechanism succeed. It is to discover which ideas survive careful examination.

What Would Count as Stronger Evidence?

Consider a hypothetical experiment intended to measure a tiny gravitational effect.

A credible progression would include a clearly defined theoretical prediction, independently checked calculations, an instrument capable of resolving the predicted signal, and an uncertainty budget covering known disturbances.

The experiment would also need suitable controls, repeatability, and a way to distinguish the predicted effect from ordinary environmental or instrumental behavior.

If a physical signal were eventually measured, we would still need to ask whether the measurement supports the particular model or whether another explanation fits the evidence equally well.

That is how a speculative idea can gradually become a testable scientific proposition.

So What Have We Actually Proven?

When a simulation works, we may have demonstrated that:

  • A mathematical model produces a particular prediction under specified assumptions.
  • A numerical implementation reproduces that prediction within known tolerances.
  • The result is stable under selected computational tests.
  • The model implies measurable consequences, physical constraints, or possible contradictions.

Each conclusion must be supported by the tests actually performed.

What we have not automatically demonstrated is that the modeled phenomenon exists, that the required physical conditions can be produced, or that the proposed technology will work.

That distinction does not diminish simulation research.

It gives the research its proper meaning.

The Larger Lesson

The universe is not obligated to behave according to our most interesting mathematical ideas.

But mathematics gives us a remarkable way to formulate questions, discover consequences, expose contradictions, and design experiments that can eventually confront those ideas with reality.

At Beyond the Light Barrier, we want to explore unconventional possibilities without lowering the standard of evidence required to accept them.

A successful simulation is not the finish line.

Sometimes it is the first reliable indication that we have finally learned how to ask the next question.

And sometimes the most important answer is that a proposed path does not work.

Both outcomes move the research forward.

Sources and Further Reading

  2. Beyond the Light Barrier — Research State v1.11. Dated project record of WC, WD, numerical investigations, limitations, and verification status.
  3. Beyond the Light Barrier — Verification Roadmap v1.1. Independent reproduction, detector credibility, forward-research gates, and physical precursor requirements.
  4. Beyond the Light Barrier — Software Development Standards v1.1. Numerical reproducibility, cross-platform testing, provenance, and software verification requirements.
  5. National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (2019). Reproducibility and Replicability in Science. National Academies Press. https://doi.org/10.17226/25303
